_comment: The words this site's own question bank tests, plus a few more at the same level. Edit freely; vocab.html reads this file directly.

words.meaning: to end something officially and for good
words.sentence: Our town voted to abolish the library card fee, so borrowing books is free now.
words.hook: Abolish rhymes with demolish, and both knock something down for good.

words.meaning: sudden and without warning
words.sentence: The bus made an abrupt stop and my backpack slid all the way down the aisle.
words.hook: Same 'rupt' as interrupt - something breaks off with no warning.

words.meaning: able to move quickly and easily
words.sentence: The agile point guard darted past three defenders and scored an easy layup.
words.hook: Agile sounds like agility, what you need on an obstacle course.

words.meaning: able to be understood in more than one way
words.sentence: Her ambiguous text said only 'maybe later', so nobody knew if she was coming.
words.hook: 'Ambi' means both, like ambidextrous - it points both ways at once.

words.meaning: friendly and easy to get along with
words.sentence: Our amiable neighbor waves at everyone, even at the mail truck.
words.hook: Ami is French for friend, and it is sitting right inside the word.

words.meaning: more than enough
words.sentence: We packed ample food for the camping trip and still had two full bags on Sunday.
words.hook: Amplify shares its root - ample means made large, past what you need.

words.meaning: very old and no longer used today
words.sentence: The letter used archaic words like thee and thou that nobody says now.
words.hook: Arch sounds ancient - think of arches on old Roman ruins.

words.meaning: boldly daring, even reckless
words.sentence: His audacious plan was to bike all twenty miles to the beach before sunrise.
words.hook: The adjective for audacity - nerve enough to actually try it.

words.meaning: bold nerve to do something risky or rude
words.sentence: She had the audacity to argue with the referee in front of everyone.
words.hook: Think of a kid bold enough to talk back to a teacher.

words.meaning: loud enough to be heard
words.sentence: Her whisper was barely audible over the noise in the cafeteria.
words.hook: Same 'aud' as audio and audience - all about hearing.

words.meaning: bare and empty, with nothing growing
words.sentence: Nothing grew in the barren field behind the school, not even weeds.
words.hook: Barren sounds like bare - picture a bare, empty field.

words.meaning: kind and generous toward others
words.sentence: The benevolent neighbor paid for our whole team's new uniforms.
words.hook: 'Bene' means good, like benefit - a good-hearted person.

words.meaning: completely confused
words.sentence: The bewildered freshman stood in the hall holding a schedule with no room numbers.
words.hook: Picture someone lost in a wild forest with no trail - be-wild-ered.

words.meaning: having a dull edge, not able to cut
words.sentence: The blunt scissors would not cut the poster board no matter how hard I pressed.
words.hook: Picture a pencil worn down to a flat, rounded tip.

words.meaning: extremely smart or impressive
words.sentence: Her brilliant science project solved a problem the teacher had never thought about.
words.hook: A brilliant light shines, and a brilliant mind shines too.

words.meaning: quick and lively
words.sentence: We took a brisk walk around the block and were back before the pizza arrived.
words.hook: Brisk sounds like whisk - short, snappy and quick.

words.meaning: honest and open, even when it is hard
words.sentence: He was candid about failing the quiz instead of making up excuses.
words.hook: A candid photo catches you being real, not posing.

words.meaning: careful to avoid danger or mistakes
words.sentence: She was cautious on the icy sidewalk and took very small steps.
words.hook: Think of a yellow CAUTION sign telling you to slow down.

words.meaning: happy and full of good feeling
words.sentence: His cheerful smile made the whole bus ride feel shorter.
words.hook: Cheer, like cheering at a game - full of cheer.

words.meaning: to gently persuade someone to do something
words.sentence: It took my brother ten minutes to coax the puppy out from behind the dryer.
words.hook: You coax with a soft voice and a treat, never with a shout.

words.meaning: clear and easy to follow
words.sentence: Her essay was coherent, so every paragraph led smoothly into the next.
words.hook: Co-here means sticking together - ideas that stick together make sense.

words.meaning: extremely large
words.sentence: The colossal wave at the water park knocked everyone off their feet.
words.hook: Think of the Colosseum, a giant stone arena in Rome.

words.meaning: willing to obey or go along with rules
words.sentence: The compliant students followed every rule the substitute teacher gave them.
words.hook: Compliant people comply - they do what they are asked.

words.meaning: to hide something from view
words.sentence: He tried to conceal the dent by parking that side of the car against the fence.
words.hook: Conceal ends in 'seal' - sealed away where nobody can see it.

words.meaning: short and clear, with no wasted words
words.sentence: Coach gave one concise instruction at halftime: pass more.
words.hook: Same 'cise' as scissors - the extra words are cut away.

words.meaning: to say strongly that something is very wrong
words.sentence: The principal condemned the prank and called it cruel and unacceptable.
words.hook: A judge condemns a criminal with strong words of blame.

words.meaning: to comfort someone who is sad
words.sentence: She stayed after the game to console the goalie who had let in the last shot.
words.hook: Think of a consolation prize, handed over to make a loser feel better.

words.meaning: easy to notice and standing out
words.sentence: The bright orange cast on his arm made him conspicuous in every team photo.
words.hook: Same root as spectacles and inspect - you cannot help seeing it.

words.meaning: showing bravery when facing fear or danger
words.sentence: It was courageous of him to speak up when everyone else stayed silent.
words.hook: Courage comes from 'cor', the Latin word for heart.

words.meaning: polite and showing good manners
words.sentence: The courteous host offered every guest a drink before she sat down herself.
words.hook: Courteous behavior is what you would show in a royal court.

words.meaning: packed tightly together
words.sentence: The forest was so dense that we could barely squeeze between the trees.
words.hook: Think of a crowded hallway with no room to move.

words.meaning: to discourage someone from doing something
words.sentence: One motion-sensor light was enough to deter people from cutting through our yard.
words.hook: 'Terr' as in terrify - you scare someone off the idea before they act.

words.meaning: hardworking and steady in effort
words.sentence: She was diligent about her paper route and never missed a house, even in the rain.
words.hook: Picture the one person still working after everyone else has quit.

words.meaning: gloomy, dark and depressing
words.sentence: The dismal gray sky made our field trip feel like a punishment.
words.hook: Dismal days are dim - both start with the same sound.

words.meaning: to drive something away until none of it is left
words.sentence: One look at the practice schedule dispelled his hope of a free Saturday.
words.hook: The dis- means away, the same one in dismiss - you send the doubt packing.

words.meaning: extreme and far-reaching
words.sentence: Cutting the season from twelve games down to four was a drastic decision.
words.hook: Drastic measures are the ones you take when nothing small will do.

words.meaning: open to doubt; not to be trusted or believed
words.sentence: His excuse for missing practice was dubious, and nobody on the team quite believed it.
words.hook: Dubious begins like double - you are of two minds about it and cannot pick a side.

words.meaning: to shrink little by little
words.sentence: Our snack supply dwindled until a single granola bar was left by Thursday.
words.hook: Picture a candle burning down, getting smaller and smaller.

words.meaning: speaking clearly and beautifully
words.sentence: Her eloquent speech at the assembly had the whole gym listening closely.
words.hook: Eloquent sounds like elegant - elegant speaking.

words.meaning: to copy someone you admire
words.sentence: He tried to emulate his older brother's jump shot at every practice.
words.hook: Emulate sounds like imitate, and it means almost the same thing.

words.meaning: weak and lacking force
words.sentence: His feeble excuse for missing the bus convinced nobody on the team.
words.hook: A frail body is the everyday trap - a feeble excuse is simply a weak one.

words.meaning: to pretend to have a feeling you do not have
words.sentence: He tried to feign a stomachache, but the smell of pancakes gave him away.
words.hook: A feint in boxing is a fake punch, and it comes from this same word.

words.meaning: changing your mind or your loyalty often and for no good reason
words.sentence: March weather is fickle, sunny at noon and snowing by dinner.
words.hook: Picture a flag that swings with every gust - a fickle friend turns the same way.

words.meaning: perfect, with nothing wrong at all
words.sentence: Her flawless gymnastics routine earned a perfect score from every judge.
words.hook: Flaw plus less - not a single flaw in it.

words.meaning: lasting only a very short time
words.sentence: We got a fleeting glimpse of the deer before it ran away.
words.hook: Something that flees runs off fast, and so does a fleeting moment.

words.meaning: so difficult or powerful that it inspires fear
words.sentence: The state champions were a formidable opponent for us in the first round.
words.hook: Do not be fooled by 'formal' hiding inside - the root here is fear.

words.meaning: to help something grow or develop
words.sentence: The new art club was started to foster friendships between the grades.
words.hook: A foster family takes a child in and helps that child grow.

words.meaning: easily broken or damaged
words.sentence: The fragile ornament shattered the second it slipped from my hands.
words.hook: FRAGILE is stamped on boxes so movers handle them gently.

words.meaning: extremely cold
words.sentence: The frigid wind at the bus stop made my fingers go numb.
words.hook: Frigid - think refrigerator, where things stay ice cold.

words.meaning: careful with money, not wasteful
words.sentence: My frugal grandmother saves every coupon and never pays full price.
words.hook: Think of a frugal shopper clipping coupons.

words.meaning: having no chance of working
words.sentence: Studying five minutes before the test was futile, and he failed anyway.
words.hook: Like scooping water out of a boat that still has a hole.

words.meaning: very thin from hunger, illness or exhaustion
words.sentence: The stray dog was gaunt when we found it, with every rib showing.
words.hook: Gaunt rhymes with haunt - picture a hollow-cheeked ghost.

words.meaning: real and sincere, not faked
words.sentence: Her surprise was genuine, since she had no idea we were hiding in the kitchen.
words.hook: A genuine leather jacket is the real thing, not an imitation.

words.meaning: friendly and enjoying being around people
words.sentence: The gregarious new kid knew half the school by the end of lunch.
words.hook: Think of a group - gregarious people flock together like a herd.

words.meaning: to keep a feeling or a thought inside you for a long time
words.sentence: She harbored a suspicion about the missing money for weeks before she said anything.
words.hook: A harbor holds ships in one place, and a harbored feeling stays docked inside you.

words.meaning: done in a hurry, without enough thought
words.sentence: A hasty glance at the map sent us three blocks in the wrong direction.
words.hook: Haste makes waste - same word and the same warning.

words.meaning: unfriendly and ready to fight
words.sentence: The other team was hostile, glaring at us and shoving during warmups.
words.hook: A hostile crowd acts like an enemy crowd.

words.meaning: extremely large
words.sentence: An immense pile of leaves filled the whole corner of the yard by October.
words.hook: 'Mens' means measure, so immense is more than you could measure.

words.meaning: about to happen very soon
words.sentence: With dark clouds overhead, a storm felt imminent, so practice was canceled.
words.hook: Imminent starts like immediate - both mean right away.

words.meaning: not favoring one side over another
words.sentence: An impartial neighbor judged the pie contest, since both our moms had entered.
words.hook: 'Im' means not, so an impartial judge takes no part on either side.

words.meaning: a lack of interest or caring
words.sentence: He shrugged with indifference when his team lost the championship game.
words.hook: It makes no difference to you - that is indifference.

words.meaning: not caring one way or the other
words.sentence: He shrugged, indifferent to which movie we picked, and let his sister choose.
words.hook: The adjective form of indifference - it makes no difference to you.

words.meaning: clumsy and lacking skill
words.sentence: I am so inept at drawing that my dog looked like a couch.
words.hook: 'In' means not, so this is not skilled.

words.meaning: certain to happen and impossible to avoid
words.sentence: With the score forty to nothing and two minutes left, our loss was inevitable.
words.hook: 'In' means not and the rest means avoidable - there is no dodging it.

words.meaning: lower in quality or rank
words.sentence: The cheap cleats were inferior to my old ones and fell apart quickly.
words.hook: 'Infer' here means below, the opposite of superior.

words.meaning: rude and disrespectful on purpose
words.sentence: His insolent reply to the teacher earned him a trip to the office.
words.hook: Picture an eye roll and a smirk aimed at an adult.

words.meaning: to start or stir up something, usually trouble
words.sentence: He instigated the food fight and then looked shocked when the trays started flying.
words.hook: Not investigate - to instigate is to start the trouble, not look into it.

words.meaning: having many small parts, complicated
words.sentence: The intricate model ship had hundreds of tiny pieces glued together.
words.hook: Intricate designs are tricky - both hold the letters t-r-i-c.

words.meaning: extremely happy and celebrating
words.sentence: The jubilant crowd stormed the field after our last-second touchdown.
words.hook: Jubilant sounds like jubilee, which is a huge celebration.

words.meaning: quick to notice what others miss
words.sentence: A keen birdwatcher, my aunt spots a hawk on a wire before anyone else does.
words.hook: Eager is the everyday sense and the trap - a keen eye is a sharp one.

words.meaning: faithful and sticking by someone
words.sentence: He stayed a loyal fan of the team through six losing seasons.
words.hook: Picture a dog waiting by the door all day for one person.

words.meaning: wanting to hurt or harm someone
words.sentence: The malicious rumor was started just to embarrass her in front of friends.
words.hook: 'Mal' means bad, like malfunction - a bad-hearted person.

words.meaning: very small in amount, not enough
words.sentence: The meager portion of fries left me hungry an hour later.
words.hook: Picture one thin slice of pizza split among four kids.

words.meaning: extremely careful about every small detail
words.sentence: My grandfather is meticulous with his tools and wipes each one before hanging it up.
words.hook: Picture someone lining up pencils until all the tips are perfectly even.

words.meaning: ordinary and everyday, nothing special
words.sentence: Most of the job was mundane: sorting mail and refilling the copier.
words.hook: 'Mundus' means world - mundane things belong to the ordinary world.

words.meaning: quick and light in movement
words.sentence: Her nimble fingers braided the whole rope in under a minute.
words.hook: Nimble fingers, nimble feet - both move lightly and fast.

words.meaning: widely known for something bad
words.sentence: That corner is notorious for the crashes that happen there every winter.
words.hook: Famous, but only for the wrong reasons.

words.meaning: new and unlike anything tried before
words.sentence: Taping the map to the ceiling was a novel way to study for the geography quiz.
words.hook: The book on your shelf is the trap - a novel idea is a brand-new one.

words.meaning: a beginner with little experience
words.sentence: As a novice on the climbing wall, he stuck to the easiest route all month.
words.hook: 'Nov' means new, as in novel and November - a novice is new at it.

words.meaning: hard to see, understand or find
words.sentence: The rules of the game were so obscure that nobody knew how to start.
words.hook: Think of fog hiding a road you cannot see.

words.meaning: no longer used because something better exists
words.sentence: Video tapes are obsolete now that everyone streams movies on a phone.
words.hook: Picture a rotary phone nobody knows how to dial.

words.meaning: stubbornly refusing to change your mind
words.sentence: My obstinate little brother refused to wear a coat the entire winter.
words.hook: Picture a mule with its feet planted, refusing to budge an inch.

words.meaning: to leave something out
words.sentence: He omitted his middle name on the form and had to redo it.
words.hook: Think of a name left off a list by accident.

words.meaning: so strong it can almost be touched
words.sentence: The tension in the locker room before the final was palpable.
words.hook: Palpable and palm - you could almost feel it with your palm.

words.meaning: strange or odd
words.sentence: The soup had a peculiar taste, like oranges mixed with pepper.
words.hook: A peculiar thing is one of a kind - odd enough that you notice it.

words.meaning: full of danger
words.sentence: The perilous trail along the cliff made everyone hold the rope tightly.
words.hook: Peril means danger, so this word is packed with it.

words.meaning: believable, whether or not it is actually true
words.sentence: His excuse about a flat tire sounded plausible, but he had been seen at the mall.
words.hook: Sounding true is not the same as being true, and that gap is the trap.

words.meaning: to think something over carefully
words.sentence: She pondered the job offer all weekend before calling on Monday to accept.
words.hook: 'Pond' here means weight - you weigh the idea in your mind.

words.meaning: to move something to a later time
words.sentence: Rain forced us to postpone the picnic until the following Saturday.
words.hook: 'Post' means after - you put the event after where it used to be.

words.meaning: very deep in meaning or feeling
words.sentence: Her essay about her grandfather had a profound effect on the whole class.
words.hook: Think of a fund at the bottom - all the way down deep.

words.meaning: to officially not allow something
words.sentence: School rules prohibit phones in class, so mine stays in my locker.
words.hook: Prohibited things get a red circle with a slash through it.

words.meaning: successful and doing well, often with money
words.sentence: The prosperous bakery opened two more stores after its first busy year.
words.hook: Think of a business booming and money coming in.

words.meaning: showing good judgment and care
words.sentence: It was prudent of her to save half her summer earnings instead of spending it all.
words.hook: A prudent choice is the one your most sensible friend would make.

words.meaning: pleasantly old-fashioned and charming
words.sentence: The quaint inn had oil lamps in the windows and a stone well out front.
words.hook: Quaint is a compliment - old-fashioned enough for a postcard.

words.meaning: to put out a fire completely
words.sentence: Firefighters needed two hours to quench the blaze in the old barn.
words.hook: Quenching a thirst is the trap - with flames the word means to put them out.

words.meaning: shining brightly
words.sentence: Her radiant smile lit up the room when she got the news.
words.hook: Radiant like radiate - a radiator sends out heat.

words.meaning: done too quickly, without thinking
words.sentence: Quitting the team after one bad practice was a rash decision he soon regretted.
words.hook: The itchy skin kind is the trap - this rash is acting before you think.

words.meaning: to move back or away
words.sentence: We waited for the floodwater to recede before walking to school.
words.hook: 'Re' means back and 'cede' means go - go back.

words.meaning: to prove that something is false
words.sentence: One photograph was enough to refute his claim that he had never been there.
words.hook: To refute you need proof, not just a louder argument.

words.meaning: never stopping or easing up
words.sentence: The relentless rain kept falling for six straight days without a break.
words.hook: To relent is to ease up, so this never does.

words.meaning: to give up or hand over
words.sentence: She had to relinquish the team captain armband when she moved away.
words.hook: 'Linqu' means leave - you let the thing leave your hands.

words.meaning: not wanting to do something
words.sentence: He was reluctant to sing in front of everyone, but he finally did.
words.hook: Picture someone dragging their feet toward the diving board.

words.meaning: so slight that it is barely possible
words.sentence: There is only a remote chance of snow in September, so we planned the hike anyway.
words.hook: Far away is the everyday trap - a remote chance is a tiny one.

words.meaning: able to recover quickly from trouble
words.sentence: The resilient team lost badly on Friday but won again on Monday.
words.hook: Resilient things spring back - think of a bouncy rubber ball.

words.meaning: quiet and not willing to say much
words.sentence: He stayed reticent during the meeting and answered questions with one word.
words.hook: Picture lips pressed shut when everyone else is chatting.

words.meaning: a quick sharp reply
words.sentence: Her retort came back so fast that the whole lunch table went quiet.
words.hook: A retort is fired straight back at you, like a ball off a wall.

words.meaning: to officially take back or cancel
words.sentence: The coach revoked his starting spot after he skipped two practices.
words.hook: 'Re' back plus 'voke' call - to call it back.

words.meaning: to make fun of someone or something cruelly
words.sentence: They ridiculed his haircut all week until he started wearing a hat to school.
words.hook: Ridicule makes a thing look ridiculous - the same word underneath.

words.meaning: stiff and not able to bend or change
words.sentence: The rigid rules left no room for us to pick our own topics.
words.hook: Think of a frozen ruler that will not bend.

words.meaning: strong and healthy
words.sentence: After a summer of training, he came back robust and full of energy.
words.hook: Robust sounds like robot - built strong and solid.

words.meaning: not often, only once in a while
words.sentence: My uncle seldom misses a Sunday dinner, maybe twice in a whole year.
words.hook: Seldom is not never - it leaves room for the rare exception.

words.meaning: calm and peaceful
words.sentence: The lake was serene at sunrise, with no wind and no noise.
words.hook: Picture a still lake with a perfect mirror reflection.

words.meaning: clever in a practical, calculating way
words.sentence: A shrewd shopper, my mom waits until the day after a holiday to buy anything.
words.hook: A shrewd person spots the angle everyone else walks right past.

words.meaning: slow-moving and low on energy
words.sentence: I felt sluggish all morning after staying up late to finish homework.
words.hook: A slug moves as slowly as anything can.

words.meaning: dark, serious and gloomy
words.sentence: The team rode home in somber silence after their captain was carried off.
words.hook: 'Umbra' means shadow, as in umbrella - somber is being under one.

words.meaning: thinly spread, with not much there
words.sentence: The crowd was sparse, so we found seats right behind the bench.
words.hook: Sparse sounds like spare - only a few, spread far apart.

words.meaning: happening now and then at irregular times
words.sentence: Sporadic showers all afternoon kept sending us in and out of the pool.
words.hook: Same root as spore - things scattered here and there with no pattern.

words.meaning: severe and strict in manner
words.sentence: One stern look from the librarian ended the argument at our table.
words.hook: A stern face has no smile in it - picture a strict principal.

words.meaning: strong and not easily broken
words.sentence: The sturdy oak table held all six of us standing on it.
words.hook: Sturdy things stand firm - both start with s-t.

words.meaning: short and clearly said
words.sentence: Her succinct answer took ten seconds and told us everything we needed.
words.hook: Succinct sounds like cinched - the words are pulled in tight.

words.meaning: only on the surface, not deep
words.sentence: The scratch was superficial, so it healed without even needing a bandage.
words.hook: Super plus 'fic' for face - only as deep as the face.

words.meaning: moving or happening very fast
words.sentence: His swift reaction kept the ball from rolling out of bounds.
words.hook: A swift is a bird that flies incredibly fast.

words.meaning: able to be touched or clearly seen
words.sentence: A trophy is tangible proof that the season was worth the work.
words.hook: 'Tang' means touch - you can put your hands on it.

words.meaning: to damage something's good name
words.sentence: One cheating scandal tarnished a reputation the school had built over thirty years.
words.hook: Dull silver is the everyday trap - a tarnished name is a damaged one.

words.meaning: long, slow and boring
words.sentence: Copying vocabulary words twice was tedious, and my hand ached afterward.
words.hook: Tedious tasks make you tired of them fast.

words.meaning: shy and easily frightened
words.sentence: The timid puppy hid under the couch whenever the doorbell rang.
words.hook: Timid sounds like tiny - picture a tiny, scared mouse.

words.meaning: calm, quiet and peaceful
words.sentence: The library was tranquil until the fire alarm suddenly went off.
words.hook: Picture an early morning with no wind and no sound.

words.meaning: clear enough to see through
words.sentence: The transparent water let us see straight down to the sandy bottom.
words.hook: 'Trans' means across - light passes across and through it.

words.meaning: so small it hardly matters
words.sentence: They argued over something trivial, like who got the last blue marker.
words.hook: Trivia questions are fun facts that do not really matter.

words.meaning: not clear or exact
words.sentence: His directions were so vague that we walked past the house twice.
words.hook: Vague answers are foggy - picture blurry shapes in mist.

words.meaning: producing no result at all
words.sentence: They made a vain attempt to save the tomato plants from the frost.
words.hook: In vain means for nothing - the mirror-gazing sense of the word is the trap.

words.meaning: extremely large in size or amount
words.sentence: The vast desert stretched farther than we could see from the bus.
words.hook: Think of the ocean stretching past the horizon.

words.meaning: to check that something is true
words.sentence: The coach called both parents to verify that we really had a ride home.
words.hook: 'Ver' means true, as in verdict - you check whether it holds up.

words.meaning: to annoy or irritate someone
words.sentence: The buzzing fly vexed him so much that he gave up on reading.
words.hook: Picture a mosquito you cannot swat - that is what vexes you.

words.meaning: bright, colorful and full of energy
words.sentence: The vibrant mural outside the gym made the hallway feel alive.
words.hook: Vibrant colors almost seem to vibrate off the page.

words.meaning: watchful and alert to danger
words.sentence: The lifeguard stayed vigilant even when only two swimmers were left in the pool.
words.hook: A vigil is a night spent watching, and a vigilant person keeps watch.

words.meaning: bright and clear enough to picture
words.sentence: She gave such a vivid description of the beach that I could almost smell the salt.
words.hook: 'Viv' means alive, as in survive - a vivid picture feels alive.

words.meaning: watchful and on guard against trouble or trickery
words.sentence: He was wary of the old ladder after he felt how much it wobbled.
words.hook: Weary is tired, wary is on watch - it starts the same way as beware.

words.meaning: very tired, often after long effort
words.sentence: We were weary after the long hike and slept the whole bus ride.
words.hook: Weary rhymes with dreary - both drag you down.

words.meaning: to come through something difficult without being destroyed
words.sentence: The small bookstore weathered two hard years and is still open on Main Street.
words.hook: The same word as rain and wind: to weather something is to stand out in it and still be standing after.
